Natural selection is the differential survival and reproduction of individuals due to differences in phenotype. It is a key mechanism of evolution, the change in the heritable traits characteristic of a population over generations. Charles Darwin popularised the term "natural selection", contrasting it with artificial selection, which in his view is intentional, whereas natural selection is not. Variation exists within all populations of organisms. This occurs partly because random mutations arise in the genome of an individual organism, and their offspring can inherit such mutations. Throughout the lives of the individuals, their genomes interact with their environments to cause variations in traits. The environment of a genome includes the molecular biology in the cell, other cells, other individuals, populations, species, as well as the abiotic environment. Because individuals with certain variants of the trait tend to survive and reproduce more than individuals with other less successful variants, the population evolves. Other factors affecting reproductive success include sexual selection (now often included in natural selection) and fecundity selection. Natural selection acts on the phenotype, the characteristics of the organism which actually interact with the environment, but the genetic (heritable) basis of any phenotype that gives that phenotype a reproductive advantage may become more common in a population. Over time, this process can result in populations that specialise for particular ecological niches (microevolution) and may eventually result in speciation (the emergence of new species, macroevolution). In other words, natural selection is a key process in the evolution of a population. Natural selection is a cornerstone of modern biology. The concept, published by Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in a joint presentation of papers in 1858, was elaborated in Darwin's influential 1859 book On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life. He described natural selection as analogous to artificial selection, a process by which animals and plants with traits considered desirable by human breeders are systematically favoured for reproduction. The concept of natural selection originally developed in the absence of a valid theory of heredity; at the time of Darwin's writing, science had yet to develop modern theories of genetics. The union of traditional Darwinian evolution with subsequent discoveries in classical genetics formed the modern synthesis of the mid-20th century. The addition of molecular genetics has led to evolutionary developmental biology, which explains evolution at the molecular level. While genotypes can slowly change by random genetic drift, natural selection remains the primary explanation for adaptive evolution.

Moravec's paradox is the observation by artificial intelligence and robotics researchers that, contrary to traditional assumptions, reasoning requires very little computation, but sensorimotor and perception skills require enormous computational resources. The principle was articulated by Hans Moravec, Rodney Brooks, Marvin Minsky and others in the 1980s. Moravec wrote in 1988, "it is comparatively easy to make computers exhibit adult level performance on intelligence tests or playing checkers, and difficult or impossible to give them the skills of a one-year-old when it comes to perception and mobility". Similarly, Minsky emphasized that the most difficult human skills to reverse engineer are those that are below the level of conscious awareness. "In general, we're least aware of what our minds do best", he wrote, and added "we're more aware of simple processes that don't work well than of complex ones that work flawlessly". Steven Pinker wrote in 1994 that "the main lesson of thirty-five years of AI research is that the hard problems are easy and the easy problems are hard." By the 2020s, in accordance to Moore's law, computers were hundreds of millions of times faster than in the 1970s, and the additional computer power was finally sufficient to begin to handle perception and sensory skills, as Moravec had predicted in 1976. In 2017, leading machine learning researcher Andrew Ng presented a "highly imperfect rule of thumb", that "almost anything a typical human can do with less than one second of mental thought, we can probably now or in the near future automate using AI." There is currently no consensus as to which tasks AI tends to excel at.

A slightly different answer : Species evolve qualities that are beneficial for survival , and passing on their genes . That 's the only reason a particular trait gets selected and passed on in a species . Humans developed large front brains ( which make us intelligent ) , because intelligence confers advantages for surviving and passing on our genes . So , humans developed big , smart brains for the same reason that we developed arms , that rhinos developed thick skin , that alligators developed an incredibly slow metabolism , and that owls developed acute vision . What would be more helpful is if they could slow their metabolism to the point that they only need to eat about once a year - and this is the trait they developed . The same goes for us . This jump is an action that needs to be processed by your CPU . One way of optimizing the code would be to inline the function like so : inline float degToRad(float deg){return deg PI / 180 ; } so that when the code is compiled it will essentially copy / paste the instructions of degToRad everywhere it 's used , removing the jump . There is a lot of this information out there already ... and I 'm sure it 's been explained dozens of times ... but here goes ..... In common experience , electrical current is transmitted through solid conductors ... usually copper wires of some sort . If you cut the wire , current will not flow . Now , take these cut ends and place them , one at each end of a small container ( say , a glass tube ) . Now remove all the air . Nothing will happen . Yet . Why ? There are no electrons for the current to flow . If you heat the negative wire , electrons will be emitted from it and move into the vacuum . Current will now flow through these free electrons , from the negative wire to the positive wire through these free electrons in the vacuum . This is effectively a vacuum tube ! The negative end is called the cathode and the positive end the anode . To make them work well , the cathode usually has a separate coil of wire near it that gets very hot ... called a heater that helps generate electrons . The anode is often a large plate ( like a catchers mitt ) to capture lots of electrons . What is neat about this is that current will flow only one way ... from cathode to anode ... not the other way . It 's like a one - way valve . This is called a diode ( di = 2 ) . If you take a diode and put a grid ( like a screen ) between the cathode and anode you can now control the voltage flow ... a small voltage on the grid can control a much much larger voltage on the anode / cathode . This is also called amplification and the tube used is called a triode . This was all discovered in the very early 1900 's . As you might imagine , vacuum tubes use a large amount of power , make a lot of heat , and are generally fragile . Over time , a lot of research was done to figure out how to duplicate the behaviour of a vacuum tube without having all those parts . This really began ( in the later 1940 's ) with the discovery of materials ( germanium , silicon , etc ) that were not conductors , nor insulators ... semiconductors . These were various minerals and other chemicals that were found to work with electric current in a similar fashion . First came the diodes , and then later , the transistor . The transistor works much like a triode , with a small voltage controlling a large one . By arranging triodes or transistors a certain way in a circuit , you can create an electrically controlled switch .... on or off . Get enough of them , and you can create logic gates and store information . Many millions of them form the basis for modern microprocessors . Today , solid - state has largely replaced vacuum tube technology . It 's cheaper , smaller , faster many many orders of magnitude . However , at very high power levels , vacuum tubes are still used in many places , like large radar or other radio transmitters .

The most popular theory for the extinction of the dinosaurs was the theory that a large meteorite , one large enough to affect the planet on a global scale , impacted Earth approximately 65 million years ago . Prior to this event , dinosaurs were among the largest creatures on the planet . Their size and power gave them dominance at the time . Mammals , smaller reptiles and amphibians mostly had to hide to survive , the former using burrows and holes underground , and the later staying underwater away from the dinosaurs . When the meteor hit , all the dinosaurs were exposed to temperatures that could kill almost instantly . The underground and water - dwelling mammals , amphibians and smaller reptiles fared much better for a couple of reasons : 1 . The temperatures were much lower underground where most of the mammals and smaller reptiles lived or travelled within , even a mere 10 inches under , survivable for those who were underground at the time . Underwater was a similar story , as heat gets dissipated much quicker in water . That 's why we have such diversity with fish and marine life . 2 . The smaller creatures required much less food . On a world where vegetation and most other life had been almost completely wiped out , it pays to need less to survive . The result was the larger dinosaurs and creatures died out , leaving the world to the smaller - bodied species , including mammals . Evolution took its course , and it 's also why the largest terrestrial creatures of today are dwarfed by their dinosaur precursors , they evolved from those small survivors . So , although devastating , the meteor collision is a big contributor to the rise of mammals , and humans by extension . As the concrete hardens, the water in the mixture reacts with the cement to form a series of chemical bonds that give the concrete its strength and durability. This process is known as hydration.

Once the concrete has hardened, the water that was used in the mixture is no longer present. It has been absorbed into the cement and other materials, and it becomes an integral part of the concrete structure.

Concrete can last for many years and is very durable, but it is not indestructible. Over time, it can crack or break if it is subjected to extreme stress or if it is not properly maintained. Hey there , aerospace engineer here who has experience in the space industry , and with college level mission design and analysis specifically oriented towards manned Mars missions . Mars one does not have the funding , technology , resources , time , scientific understanding , or technical acumen needed to pull off a mission of the caliber they are proposing . For their mission to succeed , several major things will need to change ; most are completely outside of the organization 's control . First , they will need an exorbitant amount of funds . Their projected plan is to use around $ 6 billion . Not only is this a ludicrously small amount , it 's a pretty sure sign of just how serious their program is ( not at all ) . As a conservative estimate , $ 20 billion is probably a better first guess for development of a Mars surface habitat capable of sustaining 4 people for a number of years . Cost drivers include a complete lack of appropriate Mars EDL ( entry , decent , and landing ) capabilities for large cargo , lack of a properly secured life support and resource utilization loop , launch and in space propulsion costs ( which alone would cost more than their projected mission costs to put several dozen tons of cargo on Mars ) , and other similarly large obstacles that require a good deal of funding well before their company will be able to sell the media rights to anyone ( and as far as I , or anyone else in the public is aware , no one is interested in buying to the tune of $ 6 + billion ) . Technology , science , and R & D : as I 've already pointed out , there are huge technical gaps left to completing a Mars mission , even ignoring the whole " bring your astronauts home " problem . Launch costs , Mars EDL , and life support are only the most visible and ( probably ) most costly examples . There are a huge variety of additional technical hurdles that Mars one has made little to no effort to adequately address . No human has ever spend more than a few days in an environment between 1 and 0 g 's . No one has created ISRU capabilities that are ready for industrial use and consumption on Mars . No one has used machines to remotely construct a habitat in a space - like environment , beyond self constructing satellites . No one has built structures on Mars ; the long term corrosive and erosive effects are not understood or adequately modelable on Earth . No one has sampled Martian soil , or measured it 's effects as a possible radiation shield ; without knowing how effective it is , it 's impossible to determine how much needs to be used to safely accommodate your astronauts , and thus how strong your structure needs to be to support it . No one has studied the psychological effects operating on astronauts embarking on known one way missions ; it is difficult to predict how team dynamics will play out , and how the astronaut 's sanity and productivity will be impacted . I could go on , but I think the point is clear . As far as time goes , their proposed schedule is as questionable as their budget , if not more so . With an initial funding of less than a few million dollars , they plan to have a custom built rover designed , built , launched , and to land on Mars by the early 2020 's . Let that sink in for a moment . This sort of endeavor takes many millions of dollars , and years just to develop . Their reason for optimism ? That they are going to reuse designs . To anyone who 's worked in the space program , this is a dubious way to save time and money . While it 's certainly better than starting from scratch ( in some cases ) , entire aspects of the rover 's design will always need to be re - examined , re built , re optimized , re analyzed , and re assessed for their impacts on the surrounding structure . I ca n't go to Lockheed Martin and buy another Mars rover , for buy one get one free . These things are n't bicycles , they are some of the most complicated pieces of robotic equipment designed and built . Testing alone takes years , unless you have the money to burn and risk to take to accelerate the schedule . And again , almost all of their proposed structures are going to need to be designed , redesigned , built , tested , redesigned , rebuilt , and retested from scratch , over many years and for billions of dollars . Their assessment of and relationship to the aerospace industry is also questionable . A true development plan does not consist of " We will pay companies to design and build components to meet our needs " . You ca n't go to one company , pay for a Mars rover to build your habitat , then go to another and pay for a habitat , then get to Mars and expect them to work together . You need teamwork , integration , cross compatible requirements and design considerations , communication between organizations concerned about intellectual property , profits , and competition , systems level testing and program management , clear program driving factors , and everything else that goes into making a mission like Apollo or ISS or Skylab work . To give one more , truly solid idea of just how unrealistic their plans are , consider this . To get to the moon on Apollo 8 , three astronauts launched atop a Saturn V in an Apollo CSM . The command / service module had a mass of almost 30 metric tons . It could support three astronauts for two weeks , with around 2 cubic meters of space for each astronaut . At the end of that journey , it was discarded . It had no ability to recycle food or water or air , or generate power . And it was launched on that journey by the Saturn V , the largest rocket ever to launch humans into space , a rocket that had more than twice the payload capacity of the Falcon Heavy , Mars one 's proposed launch vehicle . It took the full force of the US government , spending billions of dollars a year for almost a decade , to build the capabilities to travel to the moon , and the tools , engineering base , and equipment involved . Have spacecraft come significantly further in the intervening decades ? Yes . Has our understanding of the problems involved with a Mars mission ? Yes . Are we considerably more ready to tackle the challenge ? Yes . But that does n't change the fundamental variables : you need mass . You need time . You need money . You need expertise . You need launchers . You need organization , skill , planning , coordination , and a bureaucratic machine built to handle the legal , regulatory , ethical , and political ramifications of the mission you are undertaking . TWO : A real Rolex band has a particular tolerance that is readily evident when you handle it . It will wrap around your wrist , but will not flex from side to side . A real Rolex band is a good sign that the watch is real . THREE : Real Rolex watches tick many times per second , not once per second like most watches . The number of ticks per second depends on the model , but it 's always more than one tick per second . The easiest fakes to spot are those that tick once per second , with the second hand jerking from second to second mark , like most watches do . A Rolex looks like the second hand is gliding along smoothly , not ticking . FOUR : This is something that can not be described , only learned by experience . In relation to the " ticking " mentioned above , you can put a real Rolex case to your ear ( back of the case pressed up against your ear ) , and it makes a very distinctive fast - ticking sound that is very quiet , but perceptible if you have good hearing . FIVE : The markings on the back of the case , which I will not go into detail about here , are very specific . If you know where they should be on the case and what they should say , you can spot a fake there instantly . SIX : The glass ( watch crystal ) is squared - off , raised glass on most Rolex watches . The date magnifier is very distinctive and difficult to duplicate . Rolex specifies a certain magnitude of magnification for the date " bubble " , and it 's hard to duplicate . A trained observer will instantly notice that the magnification is incorrect . SEVEN : The glass ( watch crystal ) is often touted as being sapphire crystal . Lots of folks will reject a Rolex because the glass seems fake . However , many old Rolex watches have a simple plexiglass crystal . Lots of Rolex watches worth tens of thousand of dollars , and rare one - of - a - kind watches , have been turned away by jewelers and pawnbrokers because they do n't know that Rolex actually used cheap plexiglass way back when . EIGHT : This one almost always calls out a suspected fake . The serial number on the back is , of course , unique to the watch . What makes a lawyer more expensive ? His opportunity costs . An expensive lawyer will have more work than he has time , so he raises his billable hour rate until his workload is equal to the amount of time that he 's willing to spend working . In other words , expensive lawyers are in demand lawyers . So the real question is , what makes a lawyer in demand ? A lawyer is in demand , and thus charges high billable rates , when the lawyer has established him or herself to be an excellent lawyer . I will use the male pronoun below but let 's be clear , many women are lawyers , and there are just as many excellent women lawyers as male lawyers . 1 . Responsiveness . An excellent lawyer will be very responsive - you contact him ( by phone , mail , or email ) , and he either responds within 24 hours or he lets you know that he got your message but has n't had time to review it yet ( and then he follows up within a few days and responds to your contact ) . An excellent lawyer does this all the time , for all client communications . 2 . Project Management . An excellent lawyer can draft a document in one hour that takes average lawyers three hours - and the excellent lawyer will do it at the same quality ( or better ) . An excellent lawyer will know the usual process for things , and will plan out all of the steps for your case in a way that is time efficient - no " oops forgot that step , we need to put this part on hold until we can do that other step , " no " oops I forgot I 'm on vacation that month , we 'll need to reschedule the hearing " , no " oh I 'm unprepared I 'll need to get a continuance , " no " I 'm not yet finished with your documents but here 's a work - in - progess for you to look at in the meantime . " 3 . Knowledge . An excellent lawyer will already have a very strong understanding of his practice area in his head - he 'll remember the important cases , the relevant nuances , which resources are crucial to check . When researching , he will be quickly confirming his understanding of the law , plus perhaps ivnestigating a nuance that is new to him . An excellent lawyer 's research is specifically tailored , precise , and to - the - point . An average lawyer 's research , by contrast , will take longer and involve more irrelevant material . 4 . Experience . An excellent lawyer will have already spent his time in the trenches , learning at the feet of older attorneys - in other words , an excellent lawyer will have years of experience to draw on when formulating strategy , predicting jury / judge responses , predicting negotiation tactics , etc . 5 . Quality . An excellent lawyer drafts very tight and technically correct documents for business transactions , prepares persuasive and well - written legal briefs , provides sophisticated and nuanced legal analysis , and is familiar enough with his typical clients that he understands their businesses . An excellent lawyer addresses all of the relevant issues , giving his client all of the necessary information to evaluate the legal strategy . An excellent lawyer 's work is well - written , solidly supported with citations , entirely relevant , and easy to understand ( as much as possible given the complexities of the issues involved ) . 6 . Connections / Reputation / Social Standing . An excellent lawyer has strong relationships with the other members of the bar , and with practitioners in his field who work in other areas . An excellent lawyer has friendly ( but professional ) relationships with the relevant authorities ( court judges , administrative law judges , regulatory agencies , etc . ) . An excellent lawyer gets along decently with everyone he meets , and does n't make unnecessary enemies . In his long career , he has gotten to know the power players who affect his practice area ( state legislators , governors , attorneys general , etc . ) , and while he wo n't call in favors in a manner that violates his ethical obligations , he will call on those relationships in an effort to find solutions to his clients ' problems without having to file a lawsuit . So what makes an expensive lawyer better ? A combination of all of the things that I outlined above . Not every expensive lawyer has those traits , of course , but those are the things that typically define the best attorneys . You 'll note that I do n't mention success rate or anything like that , mostly because lawyers who possess most of the above traits are going to be more successful than lawyers who do not . While clients may be most interested in " win rates " or success stories , the truth is that you want a lawyer who consistently displays as many of the above traits as possible , because that 's the lawyer who will give you the best chance of success . A note on larger firms : many large firms have very high overhead and the billing rates of their attorneys must capture the overhead costs , so those firms set their attorneys ' rates higher than small / mid - sized firm lawyers . Individually , many attorneys at large law firms will have inflated billing rates - if they were trying to practice on their own , or at a smaller firm , they 'd be billing less . Additionally , large firms have spent decades cultivating a brand of only hiring the best lawyers from the best law schools , of requiring their lawyers to work long hours , etc . These firms have pushed the message that the pedigree of their attorneys , plus the " training by fire " that they give to their attorneys , justify the high billing rates that you see at large firms . But you 'll note that schooling does n't obviously play a big role in some of the factors that I listed above , so there 's definitely an evolving conversation among large firm clients about whether they are overpaying for legal services when they hire large firms . Second note : I have tried to outline reasons why a particular lawyer may bill more than a similar lawyer in the same practice area and in the same geographical market . I 'm not trying to say that every expensive lawyer is a good lawyer - certainly not . I 'm merely trying to explain some of the things that a great lawyer does that justify billing a higher rate .

It is based on the idea of decomposing a sequence into a sum of sinusoids, each with a different frequency and phase. The FFT takes advantage of the symmetry and periodicity properties of the DFT to reduce the computational complexity of the algorithm from O(N^2) to O(N log N), where N is the length of the sequence. This makes it much faster than naive methods for computing the DFT, such as the direct computation of the DFT using the definition, which has a complexity of O(N^2). There are several different algorithms for computing the FFT, including the Cooley-Tukey algorithm, the Bluestein's algorithm, and the Prime Factor algorithm. John von Neumann (/vɒn ˈnɔɪmən/; Hungarian: Neumann János Lajos, pronounced [ˈnɒjmɒn ˈjaːnoʃ ˈlɒjoʃ]; December 28, 1903 – February 8, 1957) was a Hungarian-American mathematician, physicist, computer scientist, engineer and polymath. He was regarded as having perhaps the widest coverage of any mathematician of his time[13] and was said to have been "the last representative of the great mathematicians who were equally at home in both pure and applied mathematics".[14][15] He integrated pure and applied sciences. Von Neumann made major contributions to many fields, including mathematics (foundations of mathematics, measure theory, functional analysis, ergodic theory, group theory, lattice theory, representation theory, operator algebras, matrix theory, geometry, and numerical analysis), physics (quantum mechanics, hydrodynamics, ballistics, nuclear physics and quantum statistical mechanics), economics (game theory and general equilibrium theory), computing (Von Neumann architecture, linear programming, numerical meteorology, scientific computing, self-replicating machines, stochastic computing), and statistics. He was a pioneer of the application of operator theory to quantum mechanics in the development of functional analysis, and a key figure in the development of game theory and the concepts of cellular automata, the universal constructor and the digital computer. Von Neumann published over 150 papers in his life: about 60 in pure mathematics, 60 in applied mathematics, 20 in physics, and the remainder on special mathematical subjects or non-mathematical ones.[16] His last work, an unfinished manuscript written while he was dying in hospital, was later published in book form as The Computer and the Brain. His analysis of the structure of self-replication preceded the discovery of the structure of DNA. In a shortlist of facts about his life he submitted to the National Academy of Sciences, he wrote, "The part of my work I consider most essential is that on quantum mechanics, which developed in Göttingen in 1926, and subsequently in Berlin in 1927–1929. Also, my work on various forms of operator theory, Berlin 1930 and Princeton 1935–1939; on the ergodic theorem, Princeton, 1931–1932."[17] During World War II, von Neumann worked on the Manhattan Project with theoretical physicist Edward Teller, mathematician Stanislaw Ulam and others, problem-solving key steps in the nuclear physics involved in thermonuclear reactions and the hydrogen bomb. He developed the mathematical models behind the explosive lenses used in the implosion-type nuclear weapon and coined the term "kiloton" (of TNT) as a measure of the explosive force generated.[18] During this time and after the war, he consulted for a vast number of organizations including the Office of Scientific Research and Development, the Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory, the Armed Forces Special Weapons Project and the Oak Ridge National Laboratory.[19] At the peak of his influence in the 1950s he was the chair for a number of critical Defense Department committees including the Nuclear Weapons Panel of the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board and the ICBM Scientific Advisory Committee as well as a member of the influential Atomic Energy Commission. He played a key role alongside Bernard Schriever and Trevor Gardner in contributing to the design and development of the United States' first ICBM programs.[20] During this time he was considered the nation's foremost expert on nuclear weaponry and the leading defense scientist at the Pentagon.[21] As a Hungarian émigré, concerned that the Soviets would achieve nuclear superiority, he designed and promoted the policy of mutually assured destruction to limit the arms race.[22] In honor of his achievements and contributions to the modern world, he was named in 1999 the Financial Times Person of the Century, as a representative of the century's characteristic ideal that the power of the mind could shape the physical world, and of the "intellectual brilliance and human savagery" that defined the 20th century.[23][24][25]

The time premium on a put option is the amount by which the price of the put option exceeds its intrinsic value. The intrinsic value of a put option is the amount by which the option is in-the-money, or the difference between the strike price of the option and the current price of the underlying asset. The time premium represents the value of the option beyond its intrinsic value and reflects the time remaining until the option's expiration date, as well as the volatility of the underlying asset and the risk-free interest rate.For example, consider a put option with a strike price of $50 and a current price of the underlying asset of $45. The intrinsic value of the option would be $5, since the option gives the holder the right to sell the underlying asset for $50 even though it is currently trading at a lower price. If the time premium on the option is $3, then the total price of the option would be $8 ($5 intrinsic value + $3 time premium).The time premium on a put option can be calculated using the Black-Scholes option pricing model, which takes into account the current price of the underlying asset, the strike price of the option, the time remaining until expiration, the volatility of the underlying asset, and the risk-free interest rate. The Black-Scholes model is a widely used method for valuing options and is based on assumptions about the behavior of stock prices and the efficient market hypothesis.

Nuclear power works like any other boiler - in a thermal cycle , water is boiled into steam , which transfers fluid to mechanical energy in turbines , then the water is pumped back up to pressure and fed back into the reactor . In the core , heat is generated by the fissioning of Uranium atoms . U-235 is a fissile fuel , meaning the introduction of one neutron tips it over instability and it breaks into fragments . Those fragments carry with them a large portion of the fission energy in the form of kinetic energy . The energized , heavy fragments ( roughly 1/2 the mass of Uranium ) collide with other particles in the fuel element and it heats up ... a LOT . The fuel is composed of Uranium pellets in the form of a ceramic , such that the fuel will not melt under these high temperatures . Uranium content in the fuel is enriched , or concentrated , to a certain percentage of U-235 . The degree of enrichment dictates how likely the fuel is to fission , due to the higher fissile isotope content . Upon each fission , multiple neutrons are released along with the heavy fragments that deposit their kinetic energy ( heat generation ) . Those fission - born neutrons are a new generation of neutrons , and lead to subsequent fissions in the core . That process of neutron absorption - fission - neutron release - neutron absorption - fission ... comprises the nuclear chain reaction . Heat is continuously produced through this process , and is directly proportional to the number of fissions that occur . Before the next generation of neutron can lead to another fission , they must be moderated or reduced in energy . When born by fission , the neutrons have high kinetic energy as they are ejected from the nucleus , on the order of 2 - 3 MegaElectronVolts ( MeV ) . Those high energy neutrons have a very low probability of causing subsequent fissions ; essentially they just fly right past the target nuclei . To increase that fission probability , they have to be brought down in energy ( moderated ) to < 0.1 eV. Smartly , moderation occurs when neutrons interact with water . The neutron collides with the hydrogen atom in water , transferring some if its energy to the water molecule , bringing it down closer to where it can be absorbed . Simultaneously , the water heats up and across the entire core the bulk process leads to steam generation . Controlling power in the core is a balance of neutron content and moderation ; how many neutrons dictates how many fissions occur , and moderation impacts the likelihood of those fissions occurring . Adding and removing fuel must be done when the reactor is cold , essentially turned off . By turned off I mean the fission chain reaction stopped , therefore fission power will not increase for energy reason . Utilities that operate the plants swap out " burnt " fuel bundles that have depleted U-235 fissile content . They do not produce as much heat as fresh bundles because the number of fissile atoms reduces as the fuel is burned . Huge cranes lift and rearrange the fuel bundles according to a precise analysis of optimal positioning . Fuel bundles , AKA assemblies , are a bunch of fuel rods held together by spacers . Rods are long pins packed with fuel pellets where the heat is generated . Pretty simple , right ? ;)

This means that the underwriter is effectively paying a lower price for the shares than the public is, and the difference between the two prices represents the underwriter's commission for managing the IPO.The underwriting discount is typically expressed as a percentage of the offering price, and it is used to compensate the underwriter for the work involved in managing the IPO process and helping the company raise capital. The underwriting discount is also used to cover the underwriter's risk in the event that the IPO does not sell as well as expected.

Word embedding is a technique in natural language processing (NLP) where words or phrases from a vocabulary are mapped to dense vectors of real numbers. The idea behind word embeddings is to represent words in a continuous, numerical space so that the distance between words is meaningful and captures some of the relationships between them. This can be useful for various NLP tasks such as language modeling, machine translation, and text classification, among others. There are several ways to obtain word embeddings, but one common approach is to use a neural network to learn the embeddings from large amounts of text data. The neural network is trained to predict the context of a target word, given a window of surrounding words. The embedding for each word is learned as the weights of the hidden layer of the network. Word embeddings have several advantages over traditional techniques such as one-hot encoding, which represents each word as a binary vector with a 1 in the position corresponding to the word and 0s elsewhere. One-hot encoded vectors are high-dimensional and sparse, which can be inefficient for some NLP tasks. In contrast, word embeddings are lower-dimensional and dense, which makes them more efficient to work with and can capture relationships between words that one-hot encoding cannot.

You have a lot of different questions in your post - I am only responding to the request for how to value the ESPP. When valuing an ESPP, don't think about what you might sell the shares for in the future, think about what the market would charge you for that option today. In general, an option is worth much less than the underlying share itself. For the simplest example, assume you work at a public company, and your exercise price for your options is $.30, and you can only exercise those options until the end of today, and the cost of the shares on the public stock exchange is also $.30. You have the same 'strike price' as everyone else in the market, making your option worth nothing. In truth, holding that right to a specific strike price into the future does give you value, because it means you can realize the upside in share price gains, without risking any money on share losses. So, how do you value the options? If it's a public company with an active options market, you can easily compare your $.30 strike price with the value of call options in the market that have a $.30 strike price. That becomes the value to you of the option (caveat: it is unlikely you can find an exact match for the terms of your vesting period, but you should be able to find a good starting point). If it's a public company without an active options market, you will have to do a bit of estimation. If a current share is worth $.25 (so, close to your strike price), then your option is worth a little bit, but not much. Compare other shares in your industry / company size to get examples of the relative value between an option and a share. If the current share price is worth $.35, then your option is worth about $.05 [the $.05 profit you could get by immediately exercising and selling, plus a bit more for an option on a share that you can't buy in the open market]. If it's a private company, then you need to be very clear on how shares are to be valued, and what methods you have available to sell back to the company / other individuals. You can then consider as per above, how to value the option for a share, vs the share itself. Without a clear way to sell your shares of a private company [ideally through a sale directly back to the company that you are able to force them to agree on; ie: the company will buyback shares at 5x Net income for the previous year, or something like that], then the value of a small number of shares is very nebulous. There is an extremely limited market for shares of private companies, if you don't own enough to exert control. In your case, because the valuation appears to be $2/share [be sure that these are the same share classes you have the option to buy], your option would be worth a little more than $1.70, if you didn't have to wait 4 years to exercise it. This would be total compensation of about $10k, if you were able to exercise today. Many people don't end up working for an early job in their career for 4 years, so you need to consider whether how much that will reduce the value of the ESPP for you personally. Compared with salary of 90k, 10k worth of stock in 4 years may not be a heavy motivating compensation consideration. Note also that because the company is not public, the valuation of $2/share should be taken with a grain of salt.

When you go scuba diving, the pressure of the water around you increases the deeper you go. This pressure helps to compress the air in your lungs, which is what allows you to breathe while you are underwater. When you ascend to the surface too quickly, the pressure of the water around you decreases rapidly. This sudden decrease in pressure can cause the air in your lungs to expand rapidly, which can cause damage to your lungs. To understand this better, imagine that you have a balloon filled with air. If you hold the balloon underwater, the pressure of the water will compress the air inside the balloon, making it smaller. If you then bring the balloon back to the surface too quickly, the pressure of the water around it will decrease rapidly, causing the air inside the balloon to expand rapidly and possibly burst the balloon. The same thing can happen to your lungs if you ascend to the surface too quickly after scuba diving. The rapid expansion of the air in your lungs can cause damage to your lung tissue and blood vessels, leading to a condition called "barotrauma." Barotrauma can cause symptoms such as chest pain, difficulty breathing, and coughing up blood. In severe cases, it can even be life-threatening. That's why it's very important to follow proper diving procedures and ascend to the surface slowly after a dive. This allows your body to adjust to the changing pressure gradually and helps to prevent barotrauma.

The Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) is a federal law that was enacted in 1974 to provide protection for employees and their beneficiaries who participate in employer-sponsored retirement and health plans.

Before ERISA, there were few federal regulations governing employer-sponsored retirement and health plans, and many employees had little or no information about their benefits or protection in the event of a plan's failure. ERISA was designed to address these issues and provide greater transparency, accountability, and protection for employees and their beneficiaries.

ERISA establishes standards for the administration and management of employer-sponsored retirement and health plans, including requirements for financial reporting, disclosure, and fiduciary responsibility. It also provides for the creation of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC), a federal agency that insures certain types of employer-sponsored pension plans in the event of a plan's termination.

ERISA has had a significant impact on the retirement and health benefits landscape in the United States, and it continues to be an important source of protection for employees and their beneficiaries.

The brain is essentially billions and billions of neurons . Any thought or perception that you have and ever will have us just a certain pattern of activation of a particular set of neurons . When you learn things , you essentially repeatedly activate the same set of neurons over and over again . This causes a transformation in the excitability of those neurons ( called long term potentiation ) . Now the next time you try to remember that , it will be much easier ( at a submicroscopic level , it will take less signalling by the brain to activate the neurons ) . Now , you have many parts of your brain that is essential for memory . These produce your working memory ( short term memory of the right here and right now ) and long term memory . Sometimes when you 're experiencing something , you may be distracted and not attentive . You will be hearing and seeing it but your brain is n't utilising that information to convert it to long term memory . In that regard , your memory was n't even formed in the first place . For example , you 're deeply concentrating playing a computer game and someone 's talking to you about their day . You nod and go uh huh , but then when you take a pause from playing games , you realise you have no idea what the other person said . If you do convert something from short term memory to long term memory , you are not guaranteed to be able to remember it . Think back to high school where you did really well in a subject . Now how much of that subject do you remember today ? This is because you need to continue strengthening the neurons over time . Not accessing memories can cause the connections to degrade for lack of a better word . But if you re - learn something , you will continue to strengthen them . I will need to stop here and also point out there are different types of memories - implicit and declarative . These are also handled by different parts of the brain . Implicit memories contain tasks and procedures that you do ( eg swimming or riding a bike ) . These are pretty resistant to loss . Decorative memory can be divided into semantic and episodic . Semantic memories are facts and figures of knowledge whereas episodic contains the events of your life . As these involve different areas of your brain , they have different strengths in encoding . Furthermore , different disease processes can affect different areas at different rates , so you might forget what an apple looks like , but you may still able to play the piano even if you do n't remember ever learning to .

This is a tricky question to answer because the terms can be easily confused . First , let 's clarify exactly what refresh rate is . Refresh rate refers to how often the screen is sent a signal from the onboard computer to update the pixels on it , and it 's measured in Hertz ( Hz ) . This is not the same as the framerate of the content you are watching , which is measured in frames per second ( fps ) and is a lot slower . This is also not the same as the " 600Hz " number bandied about by the Plasma TV makers . Before you continue , please read my explanation on [ how LCD , LED and Plasma TVs work ] ( URL0 ) . It 'll help you understand the next part better . So this " 600Hz " number refers to the subfield rate of the set . This is where the screen sends a brief charge to each pixel to make it light up . It is n't actually changing any of the pixels , it 's just making them light up , over and over and over again , 600 times a second . This is done to maintain a smooth , constant level of light output . If it happened any slower , you would start to see the entire screen flicker very slightly , enough to bother you . Now the refresh rate is the rate at which pixels can actually be changed by the onboard computer in response to the incoming video signal . On Plasma TVs , this is typically between 48Hz and 60Hz , depending on the framerate of the content . On LCD TVs , it 's between 60Hz and 240Hz ( but LCDs do it in a somewhat hacky way ; [ click here for more deets ] ( URL1 ) ) . " But , " I hear you cry , " if movies are shot at 24fps and they look super smooth , why do we need faster refresh rates ? Surely 24fps is more than enough ? " No , not really . You see , there is a bit of brain hacking going on that allows movie makers to get away with 24fps . Movies are shot on film -- basically a series of still photographs -- with each frame exposed for 1/24th of a second . 1/24th of a second is a long time for a a photo ; most still cameras keep the shutter open for 1/200th of a second at most . If you took a picture with a 1/24 second shutter , the picture would come out blurry as fuck because of camera shake . And that 's exactly what happens with film ; each frame is blurry . It 's called motion blur . When the frames are played back one after another very rapidly ( ie . when you 're watching the film ) your brain is able to compensate and remove the blur . But that does n't work when there 's no motion blur ( as is the case with anything not shot on film , like most TV shows . ) Without motion blur , the brain hack fails and everything starts looking stuttery ( ask a gamer with a slow videocard about this . ) And so the framerate has to be increased to smooth everything out again . So yeah , I hope that explains it .

I could go into a little more detail , if anyone 's interested . A quick primer on video coding : " raw " video is a sequence of raw images . A raw image is what the camera sensor generates . Typically , a camera sensor would use between 1 - 4 bytes to store / transmit a single pixel . So a 1080p image would e.g. take 1920x1080x2 bytes . At 30 frames ( images ) per second , that would be a bit rate of 1920x1080x2x30x8 bits per second . That 's ~1 Gbps . No one has that kind of bandwidth ( yet ) . Video coding works to reduce the space it takes to store video . So our example sensor would still generate ~1 Gbps , but I would then encode the video and reduce it to something a lot lesser . This is transmitted / stored , decoded and then displayed . This is what ALL codecs do . However , different codecs have different features . Almost ALL popular consumer codecs make use of so - called " lossy " coding techniques . What this means is that the decoded video loses some information relative to the original video . Often times the loss is perceivable ( URL0 ) , but a good codec attempts to minimize the loss . ( NB : lossless codecs do exist , and are often used in applications where there is a legal need to NOT have losses . e.g. medical , law enforcement , etc ) History / Examples MJPEG - as the name would suggest , is motion JPEG . It compresses each image in the sequence independently as a JPEG image . These are sometimes called " Intra frames " . MPEG1 - designed way back in the late 80s / early 90s . It was one of the first to standardize " inter - frame " encoding . This is key and helps save a lot of space . In a typical video there 's not too much difference from frame to frame ( think about it- there 's not much movement in 1/30th of a second unless you 're recording The Flash ) . Inter - frame coding is a technique where encoders need to store " just " the difference between frames H263 - The predecessor to H264 and designed in the mid 90s . Also maintained by the same organization as H264 ( ITU - T ) , added features like a deblocking filter ( where the " blockiness " due to compression losses could be reduced ) , larger resolutions , etc . Standardization is important to allow interoperability . However , video standards do n't really standardize how encoding should be done . They just standardize how the output of encoding should look . This leaves a lot of leeway to implementers of encoding algorithms to come up with better algorithms , while still letting everyone play the video . In effect , organizations like the ITU are gatekeepers of the larger interest of interoperability , but they are NOT deciding quality . H264 H264 , ratified in the early ' 00s was essentially an umbrella standard that took all the advances in video encoding / decoding sigproc research since the past iteration and standardized them . It added a WHOLE bunch of really amazing features . Some examples : multiple reference frames - you could use multiple past frames as reference to describe the present frame , thus allowing better compression more accurate " sub - pixel " motion compensation - so movement could be encoded better entropy coding - optimizes pixels down to " bits " by taking advantage of statistical models of the video Some of this stuff is really involved and really seriously cool . However , stuff like this involves big money , and so some of the algorithmic bits of the H264 standard are patented by various companies . For example , Cisco has a patent that involves the entropy coding bit above . So , in countries that respect software / algorithm patents , large parts of H264 are patented . A company called the MPEG LA ( no real relation to MPEG ) administers the pool . MPEG LA actively litigates people who implement H264 without licensing the patents . They charge royalties based on the number of users of a particular implementation . WebRTC , Mozilla , Cisco , et al * Thanks to all the funky stuff above , H264 is a really awesome codec for peer - to - peer video communications ( high quality , low bandwidth , etc ) . Industry standard H264 based communication stacks can cost millions . As media consumption moved away from standalone apps into the web and browsers , browser support for video codecs became critical . In 2011 ( ? ) Google released a Free and open source browser based video conferencing stack called WebRTC " into the wild " . ( Google 's aim is always to increase web usage in any way possible , so they can sell ads and make money ) However WebRTC could not use H264 because web codecs had to be open , and no one wanted to take the hit of paying for H264 . This is exactly what Cisco and Mozilla have done . Cisco has agreed to license H264 from MPEGLA and release it into the wild while paying MPEGLA for it . Mozilla has agreed to include H264 into WebRTC now that it 's open source . To tie all this together , getting H264 into WebRTC would mean that A LOT more people can use high quality video in the browser . Thus the hullabaloo .

In more precise terms , languages with many speakers and many neighbours have simpler systems of inflectional morphology , the grammatical prefixes and suffixes ( and sometimes “ infixes ” ) that make languages like Latin , Russian and Ancient Greek hard for the foreign learner . Contrary to educated people ’s stereotypes , the tiny languages spoken by “ stone - age ” or isolated tribes tend to be the world ’s most complicated , while big ones are less so , by this metric . > What Messrs Lupyan and Dale found through a statistical look at thousands of languages , John McWhorter , a linguist at Columbia University , found in a detailed study of just five . In his 2007 book “ Language Interrupted ” , he asked why certain big , prestigious languages seem systematically simpler than their ancestors and cousins . English is simpler than German ( and Old English ) ; modern Persian is a breeze next to Old Persian and modern Pushtu ; modern spoken Arabic dialects have lost much of the grammatical curlicues of classical Arabic ; modern Mandarin is simpler than other modern Chinese languages ; and Malay is simpler than related Austronesian languages . Mr McWhorter ’s conclusion , in simple terms , is that when lots of adults learn a foreign language imperfectly , they do without unnecessary and tricky bits of grammar . ( Most languages have enough built - in redundancy for grammars to be more complicated than they have to be . ) Modern Mandarin is a perfect example of a language almost completely devoid of inflectional morphology , all those prefixes and suffixes . All languages have their complexities , but Mr McWhorter believes that Mandarin , English , Persian , Malay and Arabic dialects are all clearly simpler than they used to be .

Each ear by itself can only hear how loud a sound is . However , both of your ears combined with your brain can tell the direction a sound comes from because one ear is often closer to the sound than the other ear , so that ear hears the sound first . Your brain can also tell that the quality of the same sound in one ear is different than the same sound in the other ear as the sound wave wraps around the shape of your head and the shape of your outer ears . With mono sound , there is only one channel of audio , so no matter how many speakers you have , they all play the same sound at the same volume . If you have one speaker , the sound always sounds like it comes from that speaker . If you have more speakers , the sound always sounds like it comes from a fixed spot in between the speakers . This is unusual in the real world , because imagine listening to a band where every instrument and the singer 's voice are all " placed " in the exact same position making their sounds . Instead , a more life - like sound spreads the instruments and voices in different locations . Stereo sound gives you two channels of audio going to separate left and right speakers , and this lets you " place " different sounds across different locations anywhere between the left and right speakers , making a virtual stage . If a bell plays louder from the left speaker than the right speaker , your left ear hears it first and hears it louder than your right ear , and your brain figures the sound comes from the left . The difference in how loud ( volume ) each channel plays the same sound is basically how stereo sound works . For recordings in the ' 60s , sound engineers did not have experience yet to figure out what sounded good , and they may not have had good mixing technology that let them spread sound finely between the two channels . They often just recorded vocals in the middle ( played identically from both left and right speakers ) , drums on one side ( say from only the left speakers ) , and a rhythm instrument on the other ( say a guitar only from the right speakers ) . The thinking here is that the speakers represent the actual band members performing . In practice , this does n't sound very good because now you 're back to mono sound for each channel . If you have a piano and guitar in the right channel only , they 're now both " placed " in the same spot on the far side of the room . It sounds horrible on headphones because if the sound only plays from one side , one of your ears hears nothing and your brain interprets it in an odd way because sound in nature almost never skips one ear . Better stereo mixes after the ' 60s avoid playing sound from only one speaker . A more sophisticated trick is to play an echo in the opposite speaker if you want to make a sound play from one side only . Better mixes can give any number of instruments unique positions across the stage in between the two speakers . There are some audio tricks that expand some sounds past the width of the stage created by the speakers , and even more advanced tricks for headphones that take advantage of the way sounds change as they wrap around your head for placing sounds behind you .

When you encrypt something using a one time pad you need two things to start : the original " plain " text and a " key " used to jumble the content of the plain text The original " plain " text might be something like " We attack at dawn " . The key for a one time pad is a string of random values that s the same length as the plain text . To perform the encryption we perform a " modular addition " for each corresponding value in the plain text / key . So in our " Attack at dawn " , ' A ' would be added to the first value of the key ... ' t ' with the second ... and so on . ( Note : Each symbol has a numerical representation e.g. ascii encoding ) . What we mean by " modular addition " is that we always stay within a certain range , call it ' clock arithmetic ' . On a clock we have 12 possible values , but if we do 10 + 8 ( two numbers within the range 1 - 12 ) this takes us out of the range ( 18 ) . To keep ourself in range we ' loop back round ' . So 18 mod 12 = 6 . The same logic applies to the english alphabet . We want to stay within the range of a ... z ( 26 characters ) so we ' loop back round ' if any addition goes ' off the end of the alphabet ' when creating our cipher text . Once you ve done all this addition you have your jumbled up cipher text .

What we know as sound is our response to pressure waves in the air around us . The frequency ( how close together ) and amplitude ( the size ) of these waves make different sounds . A speaker creates pressure waves by moving a cone back and forth . By moving at different speeds and over different distances , it creates waves of specific frequencies and amplitude . The cone of the speaker has a magnet attached to it . Near that magnet inside the speaker housing is a coil of wire . When electricity is run through the coil of wire the magnet gets pulled toward the coil . When the electricity in the coil stops , the magnet springs away from the coil due to the shape of the speaker cone . Running electricity through the coil at differing frequencies and for differing durations cause the speaker cone to move sound waves at various frequencies and amplitudes . Headphones usually have very small speaker cones and very small magnets . Because of this , they are usually not very good at creating low frequency sound waves .

Imagine you 've got a stationary object emitting pulses , and those pulses actually have to travel to you in order for you to perceive them . What pitch you hear ( if it 's sound ) or what colour you see ( if light ) depend on how often a pulse gets to you . Now , what if the object is moving toward you instead of sitting still ? It 's still giving out pulses at the same rate , but now every time it gives out a pulse , it is closer to you than it was when it gave out the previous pulse , so it takes less time for the second pulse to get to you because there was less distance . To you , this will seem like the pulses are coming closer together , changing the pitch / colour you perceive . If the object is moving away from you , every time it gives out a pulse it will take even longer to get to you because it has to travel further than the previous one . This makes it seem like the pulses are coming further apart , changing your perception of the colour / pitch . It turns out that light pulses coming faster means that what you see looks more blue , while light pulses coming slower means what you see looks more red . The same thing happens with sound except with fast / slow instead of blue / red . Really they are waves instead of pulses , but what matters for perceiving waves is pretty much the same , it 's how far between one whole wave from peak to valley back to peak again . So if you imagine the pulses to just be how often a peak gets to you then the explanation fits .

Intelligence in dog breeds is a tricky question . Thing is , different dogs are bred to do different things . A doberman or a border collie are working dogs bred for problem solving abilities and a willingness to modify orders based on available information . ( A collie needs to adjust its path to herd sheep , for example , even if they 're being whistled another way . ) Chihuahuas on the other hand were essentially bred to be house alarms . Their purpose is to make a hell of a lot of noise whenever strangers get near their territory , while being small and compact enough to make their upkeep minimal . Of course there will always be outliers , individual dogs with traits contrary to their breed standard , but in general you 'll be unlikely to find a chihuahua who 's naturally inclined towards learning obedience tricks , or a collie who does nothing but sleep under blankets and freak out whenever strangers come over . Does that mean one breed is stupider ? Not necessarily . It means they 're both specialized . One just is n't specialized towards being an independent thinker . That said , I own a chihuahua . He 's intelligent enough to have a clear theory of mind ( i.e. he understands that other people and animals have different information available to them than he does ) and is capable of manipulating the cats into feeding him . He can also pick up when I do n't want the cats doing a certain action ( like messing with my laptop screen ) and will police them to make sure they do n't . However , he will also compulsively bark at anyone who comes in the door even if he knows who they are . Is that stupidity or is that just a behavior hardwired into his little brain from generations of selective breeding ? Hard to tell . Anyway . Working as I do with puppies I can say for absolute certain that there are some breeds who 're on average dumb as rocks , while there are others who 're always way too smart for their own good , but from what I 've observed this seems to have nothing to do with size and everything to do with breed function . By far the less intelligent puppies tend to be companion breeds - dogs that were never meant to do anything besides sit around looking fancy . The smartest puppies tend to be the ratters or independent hunters . Somewhere in the middle are companion hunters who listen very well but tend to lack common sense . It 's all really fascinating , actually . Edit : But yeah in answer to the question , border collies are smart because they were bred for herding which requires high intelligence . Brain size is n't as important as wiring .

Options are financial contracts that give you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a specific asset at a predetermined price on or before a certain date. There are two types of options: call options and put options. A call option gives you the right to buy an asset at a certain price, called the strike price, on or before a certain date, called the expiration date. For example, if you buy a call option on a stock with a strike price of $50 and the stock is trading at $60, you have the right to buy the stock at $50 any time before the expiration date. A put option gives you the right to sell an asset at a certain price, called the strike price, on or before a certain date, called the expiration date. For example, if you buy a put option on a stock with a strike price of $50 and the stock is trading at $40, you have the right to sell the stock at $50 any time before the expiration date. Options can be risky because the value of the option can go down as well as up, and you could end up losing money if the price doesn't move in the direction you were hoping for. However, they can also be a useful tool for hedging against potential losses or for speculating on price movements.

In a nutshell it 's like trying to display a fraction when the numbers you are allowed to use are whole numbers only . How would you represent 1/2 if you can only choose 0 or 1 ? Some you might say are 0 , and others you might say are 1 . So you 're losing information when you store the fractions using whole numbers . This is kind of how digital displays and digital cameras work to render pixels on a screen , or photograph them . Most displays are pixel based and there is a very tiny sequence of red , green , and blue squares which light up to form a single pixel ( subpixels ) and they are fixed in place . There are also pixels in the CCD or CMOS sensor of a camera , which are also fixed in place . Now in a perfect scenario , the camera distance and zoom would be such that for every pixel on the display , a pixel of the camera picks it up . This would be a 1:1 pixel ratio . But what happens if the camera has more pixels or smaller pixels , or the distance to the display is not perfect for 1:1 viewing ? The pixels may not align between screen and camera and so some camera pixels will see two half pixels , possibly of different colors , and so it will show something halfway between those two pixels in color and brightness . Meanwhile other sensor pixels may pick up a single clean display pixel and show it accurately . This difference between perfectly captured pixels and partially captured pixels is what causes the noise and screen door effect as the camera moves closer or farther away . Since the pixels are arranged in rows and columns at fixed distances from each other , we see this as aliasing or bands of dark areas or noise . The reason you do n't see this effect very much using film cameras is because they use little particles of light sensitive emulsion that are scattered randomly all over the film . They are n't lined up in perfect rows and columns like a digital sensor would be . So when they record the light from pixels that are n't at a perfect 1:1 ratio , the distortion gets spread evenly throughout the random placement of the film , instead of lined up in perfect rows and amplifying this pixel distortion . You can also have this problem with LCD and other pixel based monitors that have fixed pixel widths and arrangements . Say that your monitors native resolution is 1000x1000 ( for ease of understanding just go with it ) . You play a game that has a resolution of 940x720 . In order to get a 1:1 ratio , the monitor would need to display the game with black bars around the edges so that the total resolution was still 1000x1000 . If you wanted to play it in full screen , it could stretch the image , but then the pixels would n't line up anymore . The result would be jagged aliasing lines similar to using a digital camera . Squares would n't be perfectly square , straight lines would look jagged and not clean . But lets say that you play the game at 500x500 resolution at full screen . The monitor can simply double the pixels and use 2 of it 's pixels to render 1 of the games . The result is 500 goes into 1000 twice , and so with a 2:1 ratio , it would still be possible to have sharply defined lines and the pixels would match up evenly and the screen would look good . The same if the game rendered at 2000x2000 but the display only went to 1000x1000 . The display would simply use 1 pixel to render 2 of the games pixels and it would still look clear and noise free . The smaller the pixel size on the display though , the less this becomes a problem as you would have to get closer and closer to the screen in order to notice . On a 4k monitor , you basically ca n't see it anymore . This is why it 's always best to run a game in the native resolution of your monitor , and if that 's not possible , then running it in an even ratio is the next best thing .

So I did some queries on Google Scholar, and the term of art academics seem to use is target date fund. I notice divided opinions among academics on the matter. W. Pfau gave a nice set of citations of papers with which he disagrees, so I'll start with them. In 1969, Paul Sameulson published the paper Lifetime Portfolio Selection By Dynamic Stochaistic Programming, which found that there's no mathematical foundation for an age based risk tolerance. There seems to be a fundamental quibble relating to present value of future wages; if they are stable and uncorrelated with the market, one analysis suggests the optimal lifecycle investment should start at roughly 300 percent of your portfolio in stocks (via crazy borrowing). Other people point out that if your wages are correlated with stock returns, allocations to stock as low as 20 percent might be optimal. So theory isn't helping much. Perhaps with the advent of computers we can find some kind of empirical data. Robert Shiller authored a study on lifecycle funds when they were proposed for personal Social Security accounts. Lifecycle strategies fare poorly in his historical simulation: Moreover, with these life cycle portfolios, relatively little is contributed when the allocation to stocks is high, since earnings are relatively low in the younger years. Workers contribute only a little to stocks, and do not enjoy a strong effect of compounding, since the proceeds of the early investments are taken out of the stock market as time goes on. Basu and Drew follow up on that assertion with a set of lifecycle strategies and their contrarian counterparts: whereas a the lifecycle plan starts high stock exposure and trails off near retirement, the contrarian ones will invest in bonds and cash early in life and move to stocks after a few years. They show that contrarian strategies have higher average returns, even at the low 25th percentile of returns. It's only at the bottom 5 or 10 percent where this is reversed. One problem with these empirical studies is isolating the effect of the glide path from rebalancing. It could be that a simple fixed allocation works plenty fine, and that selling winners and doubling down on losers is the fundamental driver of returns. Schleef and Eisinger compare lifecycle strategy with a number of fixed asset allocation schemes in Monte Carlo simulations and conclude that a 70% equity, 30% long term corp bonds does as well as all of the lifecycle funds. Finally, the earlier W Pfau paper offers a Monte Carlo simulation similar to Schleef and Eisinger, and runs final portfolio values through a utility function designed to calculate diminishing returns to more money. This seems like a good point, as the risk of your portfolio isn't all or nothing, but your first dollar is more valuable than your millionth. Pfau finds that for some risk-aversion coefficients, lifecycles offer greater utility than portfolios with fixed allocations. And Pfau does note that applying their strategies to the historical record makes a strong recommendation for 100 percent stocks in all but 5 years from 1940-2011. So maybe the best retirement allocation is good old low cost S&P index funds!

Bertrand Arthur William Russell, 3rd Earl Russell, OM, FRS[66] (18 May 1872 – 2 February 1970) was a British mathematician, philosopher, logician, and public intellectual. For other things the additional time it takes for the inside to reach a high enough tempature when frozen will cause the outside to over cook . Carbon dating and radiometric dating are methods used to determine the age of objects by measuring the amount of a particular type of isotope they contain. Carbon-14 is present in all living things in a constant amount while they are alive, but when they die, they stop absorbing carbon-14 and the amount of carbon-14 begins to decrease through a process called radioactive decay. By measuring the amount of carbon-14 in a sample and comparing it to the known decay rate of carbon-14, scientists can determine how old the sample is. In radiometric dating, scientists measure the amount of a particular isotope in a sample and compare it to the amount of the isotope's decay products. The ratio of the isotope to its decay products tells scientists how old the sample is. To determine the initial amount of the isotope in the sample, scientists use a technique called isotope dilution. This involves adding a known amount of the isotope to the sample and measuring the resulting increase in the ratio of the isotope to its decay products. From this, scientists can calculate the initial amount of the isotope in the sample. Adolf Hitler , and the circumstances which put him in power , did n't develop in a bubble . Antisemitism and many other ideas that were to be adopted by the Nazis were common and widespread in central Europe during the 19th and 20th centuries . In the 19th century , now - discredited theories on race said that different races of people had certain inherent qualities and abilities , and that races could be organized into a hierarchy ( with white , Germanic European people , which they called Aryans , at the top ) . Jews , Slavs and Roma were considered to be racially inferior to Aryans and at the bottom of the hierarchy , meaning Aryans had the right to rule over them and were being brought down by having to share a country with them . Jews in particular were thought of as being natural manipulators who exploited the work of " superior " Aryans . The 19th and early 20th centuries were also a time when Europe was in a frenzy over the growth of Communism . Many people saw Communism as being something spread by Jews as a means of controlling the world . Hitler , his predecessors and his contemporaries saw fighting Communism and fighting Judaism as one in the same ; Hitler himself described the enemy as " Jewish Marxism " . This would have went into overdrive following the Russian revolution of 1917 , in which people like Leon Trotsky ( himself a Jew ) led a Communist overthrow of the Tsar . Following the German surrender at the end of WW1 , the country became a republic and an attempt at a Communist revolution took place leading to intense fighting between Nationalist and Communist fighters on the streets of major cities . To people like Hitler ( then a soldier in the German army ) , the surrender was a betrayal of the army designed to humiliate and weaken Germany . They believed that various groups - Liberals , Communists , etc - had deliberately undermined the German war effort to prevent a German victory . This scapegoat quickly became " International Jewry " , including Jews and people working for the Jews ( Liberals , etc ) . This " stabbed - in - the - back myth " would dominate the narratives of the Nazis and other like - minded parties , and easily fed into other conspiracies about Jewish manipulation of politicians and the world economy ( the Wall St Crash which led to the Nazis taking power in 1933 was , of course , blamed on Jewish Capitalists ) . After WW1 , Hitler remained in the German army and became an intelligence officer . In 1919 he was sent to infiltrate and spy on the German Workers Party , which was founded by a guy called Anton Drexler . Hitler was impressed by Drexler 's antisemitism , anti - Communism , anti - Capitalism , nationalism etc and this probably helped cement many of Hitler 's views into Drexler 's ideology . Hitler joined the GWP , quickly took up a leadership position , renamed it the National Socialist German Workers Party ( or the Nazi Party to us ) and took it from there .

Bladeless fans, like those made by Dyson, use a technology called "air multiplier" to move air. The small motor inside the fan draws in air and pushes it through a narrow aperture (hole) at the base of the fan. 2. As the air passes through the aperture, it speeds up and creates a high-pressure zone. 3. Above the aperture, there is a loop amplifier, which is a ring-shaped tube with a smooth curve on the top. This loop amplifier helps to amplify the air coming out of the aperture and pushes it upwards. 4. The amplified air then flows over the loop amplifier and creates a low-pressure zone, which sucks in more air from the surrounding area. 5. The combination of the high-pressure air coming out of the aperture and the low-pressure air being sucked in from the surrounding area creates a continuous airflow, which cools and refreshes the room. So, even though there are no blades on a bladeless fan, it is still able to move air around the room by using a small motor and the principles of physics to amplify and circulate the air.

This can be done with the use of an electrolysis cell, which consists of two electrodes (usually made of a conductive material such as platinum or carbon) and an electrolyte solution (usually an aqueous solution of an ionic compound such as sodium chloride).

Gasification of fossil fuels: Hydrogen can be produced from fossil fuels, such as coal, natural gas, and oil, through a process called gasification. In this process, the fossil fuel is converted into a gas, which is then treated with steam to produce a synthesis gas (syngas) containing hydrogen and carbon monoxide. The syngas can then be processed to remove impurities and produce pure hydrogen gas.

Biological production: Hydrogen can also be produced biologically, through the process of fermentation. In this process, microorganisms such as bacteria and algae consume organic matter and produce hydrogen as a byproduct. This method of hydrogen production is still in the early stages of development and is not yet widely used.
